### Alliteration and Assonance

**Alliteration** (repeated consonant sounds) and **assonance** (repeated vowel sounds) create subliminal music:

> "The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew, / The furrow followed free."
— Samuel Taylor Coleridge, *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner*

The F-sounds mimic the rush of wind and water.

> "Do not go gentle into that good night."
— Dylan Thomas, *Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night*

The repeated G and N sounds (go, gentle, good, night) create a sense of inevitability and weight. The line is heavy in the mouth.

### Consonance and Dissonance

Hard consonants (K, T, P, G) create friction. Soft consonants (L, M, N, S, W) create smoothness.

❌ The contract requires strict compliance with complex corporate protocols. *(hard — bureaucratic, aggressive)*
✅ The agreement asks that we follow a few shared principles. *(soft — collaborative, welcoming)*

Neither is universally "better" — the choice should match the message.

## The Power of the Polysyndeton

**Polysyndeton:** Deliberately repeating conjunctions *(and, or, but)* between every item.

> "We have spoken of the sun and the moon and the stars and the earth beneath our feet."
— Paraphrase of biblical cadence

The repeated *and* creates a sense of accumulation, abundance, or exhaustion. Each item feels equally weighty.

**Asyndeton:** Deliberately omitting conjunctions.

> "I came, I saw, I conquered."
— Julius Caesar (via Suetonius)

The omission of *and* creates speed, decisiveness, and finality.

## Famous Examples of Masterful Rhythm

### Dickens — The Long-Breath Opener
> "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair..."

Charles Dickens, *A Tale of Two Cities*

Notice the rhythm: *best/worst, wisdom/foolishness, belief/incredulity, Light/Darkness, hope/despair*. It's anaphora (repeated opening) + antithesis (paired opposites) + crescendo. The passage builds and builds, and the reader is carried by the wave.

### DeLillo — The Hypnotic Fragment
> "The smoke. The crowd. The sirens. The paper drifting down. He walked and kept walking."

Don DeLillo, *Falling Man*

Four sentence fragments. Each is a snapshot. The rhythm mimics the disorientation of the event — the brain processing in disconnected images.

### Didion — The Long Sentence That Breathes
> "I am trying to think if there is anything else I remember about the cerebral cortex, which I studied in a neuroanatomy class at Cal, an impossibly hard class, and I recall that the cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that distinguishes us from the animals, that gives us the capacity to reason and to reflect, and that is why we are able to watch, say, a television documentary about the horrors of war and then get up and make a sandwich."

Joan Didion, *The Year of Magical Thinking*

One sentence, 95 words. It starts in a clinical register (*cerebral cortex, neuroanatomy*) and collapses into the domestic (*make a sandwich*). The rhythm of the sentence — its inexorable slide from the academic to the mundane — is the argument. The form is the meaning.

## Practical Checks for Your Own Prose

1. **Read aloud.** If you stumble, your reader will too.
2. **Count the stressed beats** in your most important sentence. Prose doesn't need strict meter, but stressed syllables should land with intention.
3. **Look for accidental rhymes** — they distract unless deliberate.
4. **Check the ratio.** A paragraph of all long sentences needs one short one. A paragraph of all short sentences needs one that stretches.
5. **End sentences on strong words.** Avoid trailing off with prepositions or weak modifiers — unless the trailing-off is the effect you want.

✅ He knew the truth. It was unbearable. *(final word: "unbearable" — lands hard)*
❌ He knew the truth. It was something he couldn't put up with. *(final word: "with" — drifts away)*

topics.title: Form the Possessive Singular of Nouns by Adding 's
topics.body:
# Form the Possessive Singular of Nouns by Adding 's

Follow this rule whatever the final consonant. The possessive singular is formed by adding _'s_ — even when the noun ends in _s_.

## Key Points

- Add _'s_ to all singular nouns, regardless of their final letter.
- Avoid awkward constructions by rewording if the result sounds clumsy.

✅ Charles's friend
✅ Burns's poems
✅ the witch's malice

The exceptions are few: ancient proper names ending in _-es_ or _-is_ (_Jesus'_, _Moses' laws_), and the fixed phrases _for conscience' sake_ and _for righteousness' sake_. When in doubt, recast: _the laws of Moses_ instead of _Moses' laws_.

Remember that pronominal possessives — _hers_, _its_, _theirs_, _yours_, _oneself_ — never take an apostrophe.

❌ Charles' friend
❌ Burn's poems
❌ The cat licked it's paw.

topics.title: In a Series of Three or More Terms, Use a Comma After Each Term Except the Last
topics.body:
# In a Series of Three or More Terms, Use a Comma After Each Term Except the Last

In a list joined by a single conjunction (_and_, _or_), place a comma after every item except the final one. This is the Oxford (or serial) comma.

## Key Points

- Always place a comma before the final _and_ or _or_ in a series of three or more.
- The serial comma prevents ambiguity and clarifies that the last two items are distinct.

✅ red, white, and blue
✅ gold, silver, or copper
✅ He opened the letter, read it, and made a note of its contents.

Omitting the final comma can create confusion — the reader may momentarily group the last two items together as a pair. 

❌ The flag is red, white and blue.
❌ We invited the parrots, Alice and Bob.  _(Are Alice and Bob the parrots?)_

topics.title: Enclose Parenthetic Expressions Between Commas
topics.body:
# Enclose Parenthetic Expressions Between Commas

Any word, phrase, or clause that interrupts the flow of a sentence without being essential to its meaning should be set off by commas (one on each side, or a comma and a period at the end of a sentence).

## Key Points

- A parenthetic expression is supplementary, not restrictive — removing it leaves the sentence grammatically intact.
- Never insert only one comma; parenthetic commas always come in pairs.
- Non-restrictive relative clauses (those that do not identify the antecedent) always take commas.

✅ The best way to see a country, unless you are pressed for time, is to travel on foot.
✅ The audience, which had at first been indifferent, became more and more interested.
✅ Monday, November 11, 1918.

Always treat the following as parenthetic: years in dates, _etc._, _jr._, and non-restrictive clauses.

❌ Marjorie's husband, Colonel Nelson paid us a visit yesterday.
❌ My brother you will be pleased to hear, is now in perfect health.

topics.title: Place a Comma Before a Conjunction Introducing a Co-ordinate Clause
topics.body:
# Place a Comma Before a Conjunction Introducing a Co-ordinate Clause

When a conjunction (_and_, _but_, _for_, _or_, _nor_, _while_ in the sense of _and at the same time_) joins two independent clauses, place a comma before the conjunction.

## Key Points

- Each clause must be able to stand alone as a complete sentence.
- When the subject is the same for both clauses and the connective is _and_, the comma may be omitted if the relation is close.
- With _but_, always use the comma even when the subject is shared.

✅ The early records of the city have disappeared, and the story of its first years can no longer be reconstructed.
✅ The situation is perilous, but there is still one chance of escape.
✅ I have heard his arguments, but am still unconvinced.
✅ He has had several years' experience and is thoroughly competent.

The comma signals that the first clause is complete and that a new, co-equal clause follows.

❌ The sun was setting and the temperature began to drop.  _(Two independent clauses — needs a comma.)_
❌ She finished her work, but was too tired to go out.  _(This one is actually acceptable — shared subject with_ but _is fine with a comma.)_

topics.title: Do Not Join Independent Clauses by a Comma
topics.body:
# Do Not Join Independent Clauses by a Comma

If two or more grammatically complete clauses are not joined by a conjunction, use a semicolon — or make them separate sentences. A comma alone is not strong enough.

## Key Points

- The semicolon links related independent clauses without a conjunction; it signals a closer bond than a period.
- If a conjunction is present, use a comma instead (see Rule 4).
- If the second clause begins with an adverb (_accordingly_, _besides_, _then_, _therefore_, _thus_), the semicolon is still required.

✅ Stevenson's romances are entertaining; they are full of exciting adventures.
✅ It is nearly half past five; we cannot reach town before dark.
✅ Stevenson's romances are entertaining, for they are full of exciting adventures.

Exception: when clauses are very short and alike in form, a comma may suffice.

✅ Man proposes, God disposes.

❌ Stevenson's romances are entertaining, they are full of exciting adventures.
❌ It was late, we decided to leave.  _(Comma splice — use a semicolon or period.)_

topics.title: Do Not Break Sentences in Two
topics.body:
# Do Not Break Sentences in Two

In other words, do not use periods where commas belong. A sentence fragment — a phrase or dependent clause punctuated as a complete sentence — leaves the reader hanging.

## Key Points

- Replace the stray period with a comma and continue the sentence.
- Intentional fragments are permissible only for deliberate emphasis (e.g., _Again and again he called out. No reply._), and only when the emphasis is clearly warranted.

✅ I met them on a Cunard liner several years ago, coming home from Liverpool to New York.
✅ He was an interesting talker, a man who had traveled all over the world and lived in half a dozen countries.

❌ I met them on a Cunard liner several years ago. Coming home from Liverpool to New York.
❌ He was an interesting talker. A man who had traveled all over the world and lived in half a dozen countries.

topics.title: A Participial Phrase at the Beginning Must Refer to the Grammatical Subject
topics.body:
# A Participial Phrase at the Beginning Must Refer to the Grammatical Subject

When a sentence opens with a participial phrase (or an adjective phrase, appositive, or prepositional phrase describing a noun), that phrase must modify the grammatical subject of the main clause. Violations are often unintentionally comic.

## Key Points

- Identify who or what performs the action in the opening phrase — that must be the subject of the sentence.
- The same rule applies to introductory adjectives, appositives, and prepositional phrases describing a person or thing.

✅ Walking slowly down the road, he saw a woman accompanied by two children.
✅ On arriving in Chicago, his friends met him at the station. _(Awkward: "his friends" didn't arrive — fix as below.)_
✅ When he arrived in Chicago, his friends met him at the station.
✅ Young and inexperienced, I thought the task easy.

❌ Walking slowly down the road, a woman accompanied by two children came into view.  _(The woman was walking, but she's not the subject.)_
❌ Being in a dilapidated condition, I was able to buy the house very cheap.  _(The house was dilapidated — not the buyer.)_
❌ Wondering irresolutely what to do next, the clock struck twelve.

topics.title: Make the Paragraph the Unit of Composition
topics.body:
# Make the Paragraph the Unit of Composition

A paragraph should develop a single topic. When you move to a new topic, start a new paragraph. The paragraph break is a signal to the reader that a new step in the argument or narrative has begun.

## Key Points

- One paragraph = one topic. Subdivide liberally to guide the reader.
- A single sentence is rarely a proper paragraph — the exception being sentences of transition between larger sections.
- In dialogue, each change of speaker begins a new paragraph.

For a short composition, a single paragraph may suffice. For longer works, group related ideas under logical heads. For example, a book review might use:

1. Account of the work.
2. Critical discussion.

A more detailed literary analysis might break into paragraphs covering facts of publication, metrical form, subject, treatment, distinguishing qualities, and relation to other works.

✅ Short, focused paragraphs that each develop one idea.
❌ A rambling paragraph that mixes plot summary, character analysis, and historical background in a single block.

topics.title: Begin Each Paragraph with a Topic Sentence
topics.body:
# Begin Each Paragraph with a Topic Sentence

As a rule, open each paragraph with a sentence that states its central idea. The body of the paragraph then explains, develops, or proves that idea, and the final sentence either reinforces it or states an important consequence.

## Key Points

- The topic sentence lets the reader grasp the paragraph's purpose immediately.
- The body sentences support the topic sentence through restatement, illustration, proof, or development.
- End with emphasis — never with a digression or an unimportant detail.

✅ **Topic sentence.** The meaning is then made clearer by denial of the contrary.
✅ **Topic sentence.** The definition is expanded. The definition is explained by contrast. Conclusion: an important consequence.

In narrative and description, the opening sentence may instead hold together the details that follow (_The breeze served us admirably._), but in exposition and argument, a clear topic sentence is indispensable.

❌ A paragraph that opens with a minor detail, wanders through supporting facts, and trails off without a concluding emphasis.

topics.title: Use the Active Voice
topics.body:
# Use the Active Voice

The active voice is more direct, vigorous, and concise than the passive. It makes clear who is doing what.

## Key Points

- **Prefer active voice** — Active sentences are shorter, clearer, and more engaging.
- **When passive works** — Use passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when the receiver of the action should be the focus.
- **Identify passive** — Look for a form of _to be_ + past participle (_was written_, _is being built_).
- **Avoid stacked passives** — Never make one passive depend on another (_He has been proved to have been seen..._).
- **Weak "there is" and "could be heard"** — Replace with an active verb for a livelier sentence.

✅ I shall always remember my first visit to Boston.
✅ Dead leaves covered the ground.
✅ Somewhere in the house a guitar hummed sleepily.
✅ Failing health compelled him to leave college.
✅ He soon repented his words.

❌ My first visit to Boston will always be remembered by me.
❌ There were a great number of dead leaves lying on the ground.
❌ The sound of a guitar somewhere in the house could be heard.
❌ The reason that he left college was that his health became impaired.
❌ The experiment was conducted by the researcher.
❌ The decision was made by the committee.

topics.title: Put Statements in Positive Form
topics.body:
# Put Statements in Positive Form

Make definite assertions. Avoid tame, colorless, hesitating language. Use _not_ as a tool of denial or antithesis — never as a means of evasion.

## Key Points

- Readers want to be told what _is_, not what _is not_.
- Express negatives in positive form wherever possible: _dishonest_ over _not honest_, _forgot_ over _did not remember_, _ignored_ over _did not pay any attention to_.
- The antithesis of negative and positive is powerful: _Not charity, but simple justice._

✅ He usually came late.
✅ He thought the study of Latin useless.
✅ The women in The Taming of the Shrew are unattractive. Katharine is disagreeable, Bianca insignificant.

❌ He was not very often on time.
❌ He did not think that studying Latin was much use.
❌ _The Taming of the Shrew_ is rather weak in spots. Shakespeare does not portray Katharine as a very admirable character, nor does Bianca remain long in memory as an important character in Shakespeare's works.

Negative words other than _not_ are usually strong: _The sun never sets upon the British flag._

topics.title: Use Definite, Specific, Concrete Language
topics.body:
# Use Definite, Specific, Concrete Language

Prefer the specific to the general, the definite to the vague, the concrete to the abstract. The surest way to hold a reader's attention is to call up pictures.

## Key Points

- Readers do not think in generalities — they think in particulars. A concrete word conjures an image instantly; an abstract one forces the reader to translate.
- In exposition and argument, ground general principles in specific examples.
- Significant, well-chosen details make prose vivid — not exhaustive detail, but the telling detail.

✅ It rained every day for a week.
✅ He grinned as he pocketed the coin.
✅ All who have tried surf-riding agree that it is most exhilarating.
✅ In proportion as men delight in battles, bull-fights, and combats of gladiators, will they punish by hanging, burning, and the rack.

❌ A period of unfavorable weather set in.
❌ He showed satisfaction as he took possession of his well-earned reward.
❌ There is a general agreement among those who have enjoyed the experience that surf-riding is productive of great exhilaration.
❌ In proportion as the manners, customs, and amusements of a nation are cruel and barbarous, the regulations of their penal code will be severe.

topics.title: Omit Needless Words
topics.body:
# Omit Needless Words

Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences — for the same reason a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts. Make every word tell.

## Key Points

- **Cut filler words** — Remove _very_, _really_, _actually_, _basically_, _just_, and _that_ when they add no meaning.
- **Avoid redundancy** — Don't say the same thing twice: _past history_, _advance planning_, _each and every_.
- **Replace phrases with words** — _due to the fact that_ → _because_; _in order to_ → _to_; _at this point in time_ → _now_.
- **Use strong verbs** — _make a decision_ → _decide_; _conduct an investigation_ → _investigate_.
- **Eliminate _the fact that_** — revise this phrase out of every sentence: _owing to the fact that_ → _since_; _in spite of the fact that_ → _though_.
- **Trim _who is_, _which was_** — _His brother, who is a member..._ → _His brother, a member..._
- **Combine choppy sentences** — Don't present a complex idea step by step in a series of short sentences when one will do.

✅ We must finish the report today.
✅ Because it rained, the game was cancelled.
✅ She decided to leave early.
✅ Encouraged by his wife, Macbeth achieved his ambition and realized the prediction of the witches by murdering Duncan and becoming king of Scotland in his place. _(26 words vs. 51)_
✅ Trafalgar, Nelson's last battle.
✅ His story is strange.

❌ It is important that we make sure we finish the report at some point today.
❌ Due to the fact that it was raining, the game was cancelled.
❌ She made the decision to leave early.
❌ the question as to whether
❌ there is no doubt but that
❌ used for fuel purposes
❌ His brother, who is a member of the same firm

topics.title: Avoid a Succession of Loose Sentences
topics.body:
# Avoid a Succession of Loose Sentences

A "loose sentence" in this sense is one consisting of two co-ordinate clauses joined by a conjunction or relative pronoun. One such sentence is fine; a series of them becomes monotonous and sing-song.

## Key Points

- Vary sentence structure: mix simple sentences, periodic sentences, and sentences joined by semicolons.
- If you find a paragraph consisting mostly of _...and..._, _...but..._, _...so..._ clauses, recast enough of them to break the pattern.
- The connectives to watch for are _and_, _but_, _so_, and non-restrictive _who_, _which_, _when_, _where_, and _while_.

✅ Varied paragraph with simple, complex, and periodic sentences interwoven.
✅ A mix of sentence lengths and structures that reflects the real relations of the thought.

❌ The third concert was given last evening, and a large audience attended. Mr. Appleton was the soloist, and the Symphony Orchestra provided the music. The soloist showed himself an artist of the first rank, while the orchestra proved fully deserving of its reputation. The interest in the series has been gratifying, and it is planned to give a similar series annually. The fourth concert will be on Tuesday, when an equally attractive programme will be offered.

Recast weak loose sentences into simple sentences, two-clause sentences with semicolons, or periodic sentences — whichever best represents the thought.

topics.title: Express Co-ordinate Ideas in Similar Form
topics.body:
# Express Co-ordinate Ideas in Similar Form

Parallel structure means using the same grammatical form for items in a series, pairs, or comparisons. Likeness of form enables the reader to recognize likeness of content.

## Key Points

- Elements joined by _and_, _or_, _but_ or correlative pairs (_both...and_, _either...or_, _neither...nor_, _not only...but also_) must share the same grammatical construction.
- Articles and prepositions in a series should either appear only before the first term or be repeated before each term.
- In comparisons, match the grammatical form on both sides.
- Bullet lists should start each item with the same part of speech.

✅ Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method; now it is taught by the laboratory method.
✅ The ceremony was both long and tedious.
✅ You must either grant his request or incur his ill will.
✅ My objections are, first, that the measure is unjust; second, that it is unconstitutional.
✅ The French, the Italians, the Spanish, and the Portuguese.
✅ In spring, summer, or winter.
✅ She likes running, swimming, and cycling.
✅ The job involves typing, filing, and answering phones.

❌ Formerly, science was taught by the textbook method, while now the laboratory method is employed.
❌ It was both a long ceremony and very tedious.
❌ A time not for words, but action.
❌ Either you must grant his request or incur his ill will.
❌ My objections are, first, the injustice of the measure; second, that it is unconstitutional.
❌ She likes running, swimming, and to cycle.
❌ The job involves typing, filing, and to answer phones.

topics.title: Keep Related Words Together
topics.body:
# Keep Related Words Together

The position of words in a sentence shows their relationship. Bring together words that are related in thought, and keep apart those that are not.

## Key Points

- **Subject and verb together** — Don't let a long phrase separate the subject from its verb unnecessarily. Move the interrupting phrase to the beginning.
- **Relative pronoun next to its antecedent** — _who_, _which_, _that_ should immediately follow the noun they refer to.
- **Modifiers next to the word modified** — misplaced _only_, _not_, and similar modifiers change meaning.
- **Unscramble the sentence** — If several modifying phrases hang off the same word, arrange them so that no wrong relationship is suggested.

✅ In the fifth book of _The Excursion_, Wordsworth gives a minute description of this church.
✅ He published in Harper's Magazine three articles about his adventures in Spain.
✅ Not all the members were present.
✅ He found only two mistakes.

❌ Wordsworth, in the fifth book of _The Excursion_, gives a minute description of this church.
❌ He wrote three articles about his adventures in Spain, which were published in Harper's Magazine.
❌ All the members were not present.
❌ He only found two mistakes.
❌ Major Joyce will give a lecture on Tuesday evening in Bailey Hall, to which the public is invited, on "My Experiences" at eight P.M.

topics.title: In Summaries, Keep to One Tense
topics.body:
# In Summaries, Keep to One Tense

When summarizing a drama, always use the present tense. When summarizing a poem, story, or novel, the present tense is preferred, though the past tense is acceptable. Whatever tense you choose, stick to it throughout.

## Key Points

- **Drama** → always present tense.
- **Fiction and poetry** → present tense preferred; past acceptable.
- **Antecedent action** → if using present, use present perfect for earlier events; if using past, use past perfect.
- **Indirect discourse** → past tense in indirect speech or questions remains past, regardless of the summary tense.
- **Avoid tense shifting** — shifting between past and present suggests uncertainty and irresolution.

✅ An unforeseen chance prevents Friar John from delivering the letter. Juliet has been compelled to drink the potion, and Balthasar informs Romeo of her supposed death before Friar Lawrence learns of the non-delivery.
✅ The Friar confesses that it was he who married them.

❌ Friar John is delayed in delivering the letter. Juliet had been compelled to drink the potion, and Balthasar informed Romeo of her supposed death.
❌ The Friar confesses that it is he who married them.  _(The marriage happened in the past relative to the confession.)_

topics.title: Place the Emphatic Words of a Sentence at the End
topics.body:
# Place the Emphatic Words of a Sentence at the End

The most prominent position in a sentence is the end. The word or group of words the writer wants to emphasize — usually the new element, the logical predicate — belongs there.

## Key Points

- **End with emphasis** — save the most important point for the final position.
- **The beginning is also emphatic** — any element other than the subject gains emphasis when placed first.
- **Periodic sentences** — sentences that delay the main clause until the end — derive their power from this principle.
- A subject at the start is not automatically emphatic; the closing position carries more weight.

✅ Humanity, since that time, has advanced in many other ways, but it has hardly advanced in fortitude.
✅ Because of its hardness, this steel is principally used in making razors.
✅ Deceit or treachery he could never forgive.

❌ Humanity has hardly advanced in fortitude since that time, though it has advanced in many other ways.
❌ This steel is principally used for making razors, because of its hardness.

The periodic sentence illustrates the principle perfectly: _Four centuries ago, Christopher Columbus, one of the Italian mariners...seeking for Spain a westward passage...lighted on America._  — all the energy builds toward the final revelation.

topics.title: Sentence Variety
topics.body:
# Sentence Variety

Writing where every sentence is the same length and structure becomes monotonous. Varying sentence length and rhythm keeps the reader engaged and allows you to control pace.

## Why Variety Matters

- **Short sentences** create impact, urgency, tension.
- **Medium sentences** carry exposition and explanation.
- **Long sentences** build momentum, layer detail, and create flow.

## The Rhythm of Length

### All Same Length — Flat
❌ The sun rose. The birds sang. The air was cool. She opened the window. She breathed deeply. The day had begun. *(staccato — no flow)*

### Varied Length — Engaging
✅ The sun rose, spilling gold across the rooftops, and the birds began their morning chorus. The air was cool. She opened the window and breathed deeply — the day had begun. *(short sentence for emphasis, flanked by longer ones)*

## Famous Examples

### Hemingway — Short, Punched
> "He came to the river. The river was there."

Ernest Hemingway, *Big Two-Hearted River*

Hemingway's short declarative sentences create a flat, stoic surface tension. The brevity mirrors the character's emotional restraint.

### Faulkner — Long, Accumulating
> "He walked through the clotting which had been the snow, tramping it, feeling it pack, feeling the cold through the rubber, through the leather, through the wool, through the flesh, through the bone..."

William Faulkner, *The Bear*

Faulkner piles clause on clause, building sensory weight. The sentence's length mimics the endurance of the character.

### Woolf — Lyrical Modulation
> "It was a splendid morning. The duck-pond was smooth as glass. But the sky was too blue; the grass too green."

Virginia Woolf, *Mrs Dalloway*

Woolf alternates long and short. The clipped observation "But the sky was too blue" disrupts the pastoral calm, signalling psychological unease.

## Patterns to Vary

### 1. Sentence Openings
Don't start every sentence with the subject:

❌ She walked to the door. She opened it. She stepped outside.
✅ Walking to the door, she opened it. Outside, the world waited.

### 2. Clause Structure
Mix simple, compound, and complex sentences within a paragraph:

> *The storm broke at midnight. Rain hammered the windows, and the wind howled through the eaves. While the house shook, the children slept on, undisturbed by the chaos outside.*

### 3. Periodic vs Loose Sentences

| Type | Structure | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Loose (Cumulative)** | Main clause first, then details | Direct, conversational |
| **Periodic** | Details first, main clause at end | Suspense, formality |

**Loose:** ✅ The house stood empty, its windows boarded, its garden overgrown, its chimney cold.

**Periodic:** ✅ With its boarded windows, overgrown garden, and cold chimney, the house stood empty.

### 4. Fragment for Effect
A deliberate fragment can land like a punch:

✅ The committee deliberated for six hours. They debated every clause. Every comma. And still they couldn't agree.

Use sparingly — one fragment per page, not one per paragraph.

## Exercise: The 3-5-3 Drill

Write a paragraph using: one sentence of ~3 words, one of ~5 words, one of ~3 words:

> She stopped. The silence was absolute. Nothing moved. The city held its breath, caught between sirens. She ran.

This pattern creates tension → space → resolution.

## When to Break the Rules

- **Technical writing** prioritizes clarity over rhythm — consistent medium-length sentences are fine.
- **Extreme minimalism** (short sentences only) can work as a stylistic choice — but it's exhausting at scale.
- **Extreme maximalism** (long sentences only) requires extraordinary skill to sustain — see Proust, Saramago, Bernhard.

✅ Short. Then a sentence that carries the weight of multiple observations, layering detail upon detail so the reader feels the accumulating pressure before the next short one hits. Then: release.

topics.title: Signposting
topics.body:
# Signposting

Signposting is the explicit practice of telling the reader where you are in your argument and where you are going next. In longer documents — academic papers, reports, technical proposals — it prevents the reader from getting lost. In shorter pieces, it can feel heavy-handed.

## Key Rules

1. **Use In Longer Documents** — Anything over 3-4 pages benefits from phrases like *"This section argues…"*, *"Having established X, we now turn to…"*, *"As discussed above…"*.
2. **Keep It Brief** — *"Next, I analyse the survey data"* works; *"The subsequent portion of this manuscript shall engage with the data"* does not.
3. **Avoid Overuse** — If every paragraph begins with *"In this paragraph,"* or *"Next,"*, the signposting has become clutter.
4. **Use First-Person Sparingly** — *"I will now argue…"* is acceptable in humanities; in scientific or business writing, prefer *"The next section examines…"*.

✅ Having established the scope of the problem, we now turn to the proposed solution.
❌ In this paragraph, I am going to tell you about the solution, which I will now begin to describe.

## When to Skip

In a short memo, a blog post, or a narrative essay, signposting reads as padding. Trust your reader to follow a well-structured argument without a tour guide.

topics.title: Tone and Register
topics.body:
# Tone and Register

Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject and audience. Register is the level of formality. Matching both to context is essential for effective communication.

## Register Levels

| Level | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Formal** | Academic papers, legal documents, official reports | "It is recommended that the committee convene at its earliest convenience." |
| **Standard** | Business communication, essays, journalism | "The committee should meet as soon as possible." |
| **Informal** | Personal emails, blogs, casual conversation | "Hey, the committee should get together soon." |
| **Colloquial** | Close friends, dialogue | "The committee needs to get its act together, like, yesterday." |

## Shifting Register Inappropriately

Mixing registers within a passage creates tonal whiplash:

❌ The defendant's culpability is incontrovertible, and yeah, that's pretty bad.
❌ We must optimize our synergies across verticals — basically, let's work together.
❌ The author posits a compelling argument, and it's super persuasive.

✅ The defendant's culpability is incontrovertible, and the consequences are severe.
✅ Cross-departmental collaboration will improve efficiency.
✅ The author's argument is compelling and well-supported by evidence.

## Common Register Mistakes

| Error | Correction |
|---|---|
| Contractions in formal writing | ❌ The results don't support... → ✅ The results do not support... |
| Slang in professional contexts | ❌ That presentation was lit. → ✅ That presentation was excellent. |
| Overly stiff language in casual contexts | ❌ I would be most gratified if you could attend. → ✅ I'd love it if you could come. |
| Jargon with non-specialist audiences | ❌ We need to leverage our core competencies. → ✅ We need to focus on what we do best. |
| Text-speak in writing | ❌ btw, lmk if u can make it → ✅ By the way, let me know if you can make it. |

## Matching Tone to Purpose

| Purpose | Appropriate Tone |
|---|---|
| Persuade | Confident, reasonable, empathetic |
| Inform | Neutral, clear, objective |
| Entertain | Playful, vivid, engaging |
| Instruct | Clear, patient, encouraging |
| Criticize | Specific, constructive, fair |
| Apologize | Sincere, direct, accountable |

## Active Tone vs Passive Tone

Beyond active/passive voice, *tone* can be active or passive:

**Active tone:** Takes responsibility, names subjects, uses direct language.
✅ I made a mistake.
✅ The team decided to delay the launch.

**Passive tone:** Deflects responsibility, hides the actor, uses hedging.
❌ Mistakes were made.
❌ It was decided that the launch would be delayed.

## Hedging Language

Hedging weakens writing. Use it sparingly — only when genuine uncertainty exists.

| Weak (Over-Hedged) | Strong |
|---|---|
| It seems that perhaps we might want to consider... | I recommend... |
| I think it's kind of important to note... | Note that... |
| The data sort of suggests maybe... | The data suggests... / The data does not conclusively show... |

## Inclusive Tone

✅ Use gender-neutral language when gender is unknown (*they*, not *he*).
✅ Avoid idioms that assume shared cultural background (*hit a home run*, *sticky wicket*).
✅ Use plain language where possible — technical terms should be explained on first use.
✅ Frame to the reader's perspective: *"You'll notice..."* not *"One will observe..."*

✅ The report outlines three areas for improvement.
❌ As per my last email, I literally cannot even with these quarterly numbers.

topics.title: Transitions
topics.body:
# Transitions

Transitions are the bridges between sentences, paragraphs, and sections. They guide the reader through your argument and signal how each thought relates to what came before. Weak or missing transitions suggest unclear thinking — not just unclear writing.

## Key Rules

1. **Use Logical Connectors** — *however, therefore, in contrast, building on this, consequently, similarly, meanwhile, for instance*.
2. **Match Transition to Relationship** — Don't use *however* for an addition, or *therefore* for a contrast.
3. **Avoid Over-Signalling** — Not every sentence needs a transition word. Let parallelism and natural flow do some of the work.
4. **Transition at Boundaries** — The end of one paragraph and the start of the next form a natural hinge; use it.

✅ The experiment failed to replicate. **However**, a subsequent trial with tighter controls produced the expected result.
❌ The experiment failed to replicate. It was raining outside that day.

✅ The committee approved the budget. **Building on this**, the team launched the first phase in March.
❌ The committee approved the budget. The team launched the first phase in March. (no logical connection shown)

## Why Weak Transitions Matter

A missing or wrong transition forces the reader to guess the relationship between ideas. If they guess wrong, your argument collapses. If they must stop to figure it out, you lose their attention.

topics.title: Word Choice and Colour
topics.body:
# Word Choice and Colour

Precision in word choice is the difference between a sketch and a painting. Every word carries denotation (literal meaning) and connotation (emotional weight, cultural association, tone).

## Denotation vs Connotation

| Word | Denotation | Connotation |
|---|---|---|
| slender | thin | positive — graceful, elegant |
| skinny | thin | negative — undernourished, scrawny |
| slim | thin | positive — trim, attractive |
| gaunt | thin | negative — haggard, ill |
| determined | strong-willed | positive — resolute |
| stubborn | strong-willed | negative — inflexible, unreasonable |
| assertive | confident | positive — self-assured |
| aggressive | confident | negative — hostile, pushy |

Choosing the wrong word changes the meaning — not just the mood.

✅ She was **slender** and moved with ease. *(admiring)*
❌ She was **gaunt** and moved with ease. *(contradicts — gaunt implies illness)*

## The Ladder of Abstraction

S.I. Hayakawa's concept: move up for overview, down for detail.

| Level | Example |
|---|---|
| **Abstract** | wealth |
| | asset |
| | property |
| | house |
| | bungalow |
| **Concrete** | the peeling yellow bungalow on Ash Street with the broken mailbox |

Good writing moves fluidly between levels:
✅ He was wealthy. *(abstract — sets the scene)* His fortune was built on a single patent. *(mid-level)* The patent was for a brass nozzle that could spray paint in a perfectly even coat — the kind of thing no one notices but everyone depends on. *(concrete)*

## Sensory Language

Abstract words tell. Concrete sensory words show.

| Abstract (Telling) | Concrete (Showing) |
|---|---|
| The room was unpleasant. | The room smelled of damp wool and old cigarettes. |
| She was angry. | Her jaw tightened and her fingers curled around the pen until the plastic creaked. |
| The food was good. | The bread was still warm, its crust crackling under the knife, steam rising from the soft centre. |
| It was a cold day. | Frost spiderwebbed across the windscreen; her breath hung in the air. |

## Famous Examples of Precise Word Choice

### Nabokov — Synesthetic Precision
> "Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins. My sin, my soul. Lo-lee-ta: the tip of the tongue taking a trip of three steps down the palate to tap, at three, on the teeth. Lo. Lee. Ta."

Vladimir Nabokov, *Lolita*

Nabokov maps sound to physical sensation. The sentence doesn't describe — it performs.

### Orwell — Anti-Precision as Critique
> "The statement 'I have not been negligent in my duties' is rendered 'I have not been remiss in the execution of my responsibilities with regard to...' and then 'I have been a good steward of the resources entrusted to me...' until the truth has been thoroughly obscured."

Paraphrase of George Orwell, *Politics and the English Language*

Orwell's point: bad word choice isn't just ugly — it's dishonest. Vague language protects the speaker from accountability.

### Toni Morrison — Single Words That Carry Worlds
> "124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom."

Toni Morrison, *Beloved*

Two sentences. *Spiteful* for a house, *venom* for a baby — both unexpected, both precise. The wrongness of the word choices is the point.

## Weak Words to Interrogate

| Weak Word | Stronger Alternative (context-dependent) |
|---|---|
| nice | pleasant, charming, gracious, thoughtful |
| good | excellent, effective, skilled, satisfying |
| bad | harmful, incompetent, unpleasant, corrosive |
| thing | item, object, concept, issue, element |
| stuff | material, substance, belongings, content |
| very | *(delete; use a stronger adjective)* |
| really | *(delete; use a stronger adverb)* |
| a lot | many, numerous, frequently, substantially |
| got | obtained, received, became, understood |
| interesting | *(say what's interesting about it)* |
| important | vital, crucial, essential, central *(or better: say why it matters)* |

## The "One Perfect Word" Fallacy

Flaubert famously preached *le mot juste* — the one right word. But in practice, there's rarely one perfect word. There are better and worse choices, and the right one depends on rhythm, register, and intention:

✅ He **walked** into the room. *(neutral)*
✅ He **strode** into the room. *(confident)*
✅ He **shuffled** into the room. *(tired, old)*
✅ He **slunk** into the room. *(ashamed, furtive)*
✅ He **burst** into the room. *(urgent, dramatic)*

None are "wrong" — each creates a different character and scene.

## Verdict

Interrogate every adjective and verb in a second draft. If a word is doing real work — carrying weight, setting tone, distinguishing meaning — keep it. If it's filler, cut it. If it's carrying the wrong connotation, replace it.

✅ The investigation **uncovered** evidence of fraud.
❌ The investigation **found** evidence of fraud. *(weaker — "found" is generic)*
✅ The investigation **unearthed** evidence of fraud. *(strong, but slightly sensational)*
✅ The investigation **revealed** evidence of fraud. *(balanced — precise, not melodramatic)*
